from pypdf import PdfReader

reader = PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')

for i, page in enumerate(reader.pages):
    parts.append(f'\\n\\n===== PAGE {i+1} =====\\n'+page.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout'))
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(parts))
print(''.join(parts[:3]))

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem for human-in-the-loop NLP: evaluating interactive coding tools under realistic collaboration settings. Its empirical and evaluation-focused aims are worthwhile without requiring a new modeling algorithm.

Comparing topic-modeling, relational, and LLM-based systems on the same approximately 85,000-tweet corpus provides useful breadth. Holding initialization fixed within each system helps reduce one source of variation.

The evaluation combines consistency, cohesiveness, distinctiveness, and manual assignment verification. The audit of 1,200 document-theme pairs, with two evaluators and adjudication, provides valuable evidence beyond embedding-based metrics.

The paper clearly explains the systems and identifies concrete interface problems through participant accounts. It also appropriately distinguishes increased cohesiveness from improved distinctiveness when interpreting the relational system’s results.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate collaboration timing. Section 4 compares three-person synchronous teams with individual asynchronous coders, without describing the consolidation step that defines asynchronous collaboration in the introduction. Team size, available perspectives, and potentially human effort therefore vary with condition. Participant allocation, reuse across sessions, and experience balancing are also unspecified. The current design supports an exploratory comparison of group and individual coding; stronger claims require comparable collaborative conditions or narrower framing.

The statistical evidence is insufficiently justified. Each system has only two synchronous codebooks and three asynchronous codebooks, yielding just one synchronous between-codebook comparison. Tables 1–2 do not identify test sample sizes or explain how dependencies among themes within codebooks and overlapping codebook comparisons are handled. Treating these observations as independent would constitute pseudoreplication. The reported unpaired t-tests and 'near statistically significant' labels cannot establish reliable modality effects without an appropriate analysis and uncertainty estimates.

The main correctness result cannot be reconstructed from the description. Figure 4 reports F1, but Section 5 describes accepting or rejecting assigned document-theme pairs without defining the F1 calculation, reference labels, or averaging. It also leaves unclear how unlabeled outputs enter evaluation; Appendix D reports invalid LLM labels for 0.7–16.1% of documents. Sampling weights, allocation across codebooks, and confidence intervals are missing. These details matter for interpreting differences, especially with moderate evaluator agreement of α = 0.632.

The proposed evaluation framework needs stronger validation. Maximum-match consistency can reuse target themes and is sensitive to codebook granularity, yet final theme counts and size distributions are not reported. Centroid similarities are nearly saturated at 0.94–0.98 across settings, raising questions about discrimination. Baselines or sensitivity analyses, together with human judgments of theme alignment and usefulness, would help establish what improvements in these metrics actually mean.

Several conclusions exceed the tested scope. Richer interaction is not experimentally isolated from differences in initialization, supervision, and the relational system’s stance/morality information, so its proposed explanatory role remains a hypothesis. Broad claims about LLM unreliability and expense rest on Llama 3.2 3B-Instruct with a small prompt set and no comparable runtime measurements for the other systems. Conclusions should be restricted to the tested implementations and English vaccine corpus unless additional controls support generalization.

Reproducibility and qualitative reporting remain incomplete despite Section 9’s assertion. Missing details include the exact SBERT checkpoint, resulting codebooks, prompt-selection sample sizes, selected templates per session, and decoding settings; the promised artifact release has no supplied location. Appendix C acknowledges skipped interviews but gives neither completed interview counts nor an analysis procedure, while interview format also differs by condition. Together with the design and statistical concerns, these gaps prevent a clear Findings recommendation. A focused revision could preserve the useful exploratory findings while making their evidential limits explicit.
